Content: Tables and graphs provide visual representations for situations described by linear functions, allowing us to see the structure of algebraic relationships. While an equation gives a mathematical description of a function, tables and graphs provide data points that form a pattern of how a function behaves. A `ultext(Table)` organizes data into a neat list of inputs and outputs, allowing us to spot numerical trends from one row to the next. A `ultext(Graph)` transforms input-output pairs into a line that connects many points on the coordinate plane. In fields like engineering and economics, the ability to create trend lines from individual data points is useful for visualizing patterns and predicting unknown outcomes for entirely new inputs.

Mastering the interplay between tables and graphs is incredibly useful because SAT problems frequently ask us to translate a function from one format to another. We might be given a table of values and asked to identify its corresponding graph or given a graph and asked to find the matching algebraic equation. Because a straight line behaves identically whether it is written as a formula, graphed on a plane, or listed as data points in a table, learning how to read different formats lets us verify answer choices. When unsure of our algebra, the graph or table can often be a simple path to finding the solution visually.

The golden thread that connects equations, tables, and graphs is the rate of change. The `ultext(Rate Of Change)` measures how fast the output (`y`) changes relative to a change in the input (`x`). On a graph, the rate of change is the “rise over run” — the measure of steepness and direction of the line. In a table, the rate of change is the constant pattern seen while moving from one row to the next. For a function to be linear, this rate of change must be constant. If every time the input increases by `1`, the output increases by exactly `3`, there is a constant rate of change of `3` which results in a particular steepness when the line is graphed.

When solving SAT problems, understanding the role of the rate of change is the ultimate shortcut. The test will often give us a table with just two or three coordinate points, such as `(2,5)` and `(4,11)`. By calculating the rate of change — the difference of outputs divided by the difference of inputs (`(11-5)/(4-2)=6/2=3`) — key features of the line can be identified. Once the rate of change has been calculated, any functions that don't include the correct coefficient for `x` can immediately be eliminated. By first looking for the rate of change, we can dismantle complex table or graph problems and even forecast input-output pairs that are not given.
